title: Methods of Psychology
summary: ## Approaches to the study of psychological processes

Biological approach: studies brain, genes, hormones, the endocrine system and neurotransmitters; the role of parts of the brain in feelings, memories and emotions; over- or under-secretion of hormones; behaviour genetics looks for physiological bases of behaviour. Psychoanalytic approach (Sigmund Freud): unconscious libidinal energy; layers of consciousness – conscious, preconscious, unconscious; explored through dreams, slips of the tongue, neuroses, work of art and rituals; most behaviour is triggered by unconscious motivation. Humanistic approach (Carl Rogers): conscious experience of the present, interpersonal experiences and the capacity to grow; a person is an active, self-actualising agent with choice; congruence between self and experience; therapy through genuineness, unconditional positive regard and empathy. Behaviourist approach (J.B. Watson): unit of analysis is explicit, objective, overt behaviour and its relation to environmental stimulation; behaviour is governed by stimulus–response association and can be shaped. Cognitive approach: information processing in perception, remembering, thinking, language, reasoning, problem solving and decision making (higher mental processes); uses computational models.

Scientific research is objective (free from bias), testable, open to all, self-correcting and replicable. Observation: studying events without deliberate interference; naturalistic (natural setting, no control over extraneous variables) or laboratory (controlled); participant (the researcher mixes with the event) or non-participant (optimum distance); advantage – behaviour studied as it happens; limitations – time, effort, observer bias; Piaget's observations of his own children. Experimentation: the experimenter manipulates the independent variable (IV) and observes its effect on the dependent variable (DV); an experimental group receives the IV and a control group does not; relevant variables must be controlled – organismic (age, sex, personality), situational (temperature, humidity, noise) and sequential (practice, fatigue when tested across conditions). Techniques of control: elimination, making conditions constant, matching, counter-balancing (Group A task 1 then 2; Group B task 2 then 1) and random assignment. Field and quasi experiments are in natural settings. Case study: the individual is the unit of analysis; data from family history, education, medical and social life through interview, observation and tests; popular in clinical and life-span psychology; gives detailed profiles but needs checks of reliability and validity. Survey: opinions, attitudes, beliefs and values via questionnaire or interview, e.g. opinion polls.

Psychological tests measure intelligence, aptitude, interest and personality; a standardised test has reliability (consistency in yielding dependable scores) and validity (it measures what it claims to measure). Tests may be verbal (oral responses) or non-verbal/performance (responses as performance or behaviour), and objective (direct items, limited freedom) or projective (ambiguous stimuli – pictures, inkblots, drawings, incomplete sentences – with free responses). Questionnaire: a set of questions, closed-ended (limited alternatives, one chosen) or open-ended (free response); instructions on the first page; administered to groups; simple, explicit language; items sequenced general to specific. Interview: face-to-face interaction between interviewer and interviewee (also by telephone, internet, video); structured (framed questions with options) or unstructured (open-ended, flexible, e.g. recruitment). A skilled interviewer establishes rapport, relieves anxiety, has command of language and controls feelings; interviews are used in recruitment, counselling, marketing and attitude surveys.

vsa: Differentiate between verbal and non-verbal test.
In a verbal test responses are taken in oral (or written verbal) form; in a non-verbal or performance test responses are taken as performance or behaviour such as manipulating blocks.
What is a psychological test? Write any two skills an interviewer should possess.

A psychological test gives an objective assessment of qualities and limitations of an individual by comparing scores with others. An interviewer needs to establish rapport and have command over language (and control over feelings).

Name any two characteristics of scientific research.
Objectivity (free from bias), testability, self-correction and replication (any two).
Observation of events in their natural setting without control over extraneous variables, e.g. children playing in a playground.
An in-depth study of one individual's experiences and background through interview, observation and tests, used to prepare a case history.
What is meant by random assignment?
Every participant has an equal chance of being in the experimental or control condition, removing systematic differences between groups.
sa: What is survey method? Where can you use the survey method?

Survey is a research method in which people's opinions are collected on current issues through questionnaires, interviews, email or SMS. It is used to study the pattern of opinions, attitudes, beliefs and values, to test hypotheses about variables (e.g. after the Mumbai attacks) and for opinion polls in elections, in psychology, sociology, political science and management.

or: What are the different methods of data collection for research? Explain any three.

Observation (studying behaviour as it occurs, naturalistic or laboratory), experiment (manipulating the independent variable), case study (detailed profile of an individual), survey (opinions through questionnaire or interview) and psychological tests.

sa: What is the biological approach to study psychological processes?

It focuses on biological structures and phenomena – brain, genes, hormones, the endocrine system and neurotransmitters – to understand behaviour; it studies the role of parts of the brain in feelings, memories and emotions, the effect of over- or under-secretion of hormones, and behaviour genetics.
Compare and contrast reliability and validity of tests.

Reliability is the consistency of a test in yielding dependable scores; validity is the extent to which it measures what it claims to measure. A test can be reliable without being valid, but a valid test must be reliable; both are properties of a standardised test.

or: Explain the features of a questionnaire.

A set of questions answered by the individual; items may be closed-ended or open-ended; instructions on the first page; can be given to a group; simple language; items arranged from general to specific.

sa: Describe the characteristics of the scientific method.

It is objective (free from bias), testable again and again, open to all and verifiable by following the same method, self-correcting (errors are revised) and replicable (results are verified by similar studies in other settings).
Explain the techniques used to control relevant variables.

Elimination removes extraneous variables; making conditions constant keeps them the same throughout; matching equates them across conditions; counter-balancing minimises order effects by reversing task order for two groups; random assignment gives equal chance of exposure to all participants.
la: What are the various psychological tools to collect data? Explain in detail. How is case study method different from survey method? Which one can be used to get the opinion of the people?

Tools: psychological tests (verbal or performance; objective or projective; reliable and valid), questionnaire (open or closed ended, group administration), and interview (structured or unstructured; interviewer needs rapport, language command and control of feelings; used in recruitment, counselling, marketing). Case study studies one individual in great detail through history, interview and tests; survey collects opinions from many people through questionnaire or interview. The survey method is used to get the opinion of the people.
Describe three main approaches used by psychologists to understand mental processes. Why do we need so many approaches?

Biological: brain, genes, hormones; psychoanalytic (Freud): unconscious motivation; humanistic (Rogers): conscious experience, growth and self-actualisation; behaviourist (Watson): overt behaviour and stimulus–response; cognitive: information processing. Human behaviour is complex, so different vantage points are needed to understand it fully.
Discuss the experimental method as a scientific method. Identify the techniques used to control relevant variables.

The experimenter manipulates the independent variable and studies its effect on the dependent variable, with an experimental group and a control group. Organismic, situational and sequential variables must be controlled by elimination, making conditions constant, matching, counter-balancing and random assignment; experiments can be laboratory, field or quasi experiments.
Describe the observation method with its types, advantages and limitations.

Observation is studying events without interfering. It may be naturalistic or laboratory, participant or non-participant. Its advantage is that behaviour is studied as it happens; limitations are the time and effort needed and observer bias. Piaget's observations of his children are a famous example.
